background.definition: Plague is an infectious disease caused by the bacteria Yersinia pestis. It is a zoonotic infection seen in wild rodents. Humans, as incidental hosts, acquire it most often through infected flea bites. Less frequently, humans acquire the infection through direct contact with an infected person or by handling infected materials. Bubonic, septicemic, and pneumonic forms are the three classic presentations of plague. Antibiotics are effective against plague, but if not treated promptly, the disease is likely to result in death.

list.listitem: An average of 1087 cases of plague per year is reported to the World Health Organization from 20 countries, although the disease is underreported in many countries with inadequate surveillance.
In the 21st century, worldwide there have been 21,725 persons affected with plague, with 1,612 deaths, a 7.4% case-fatality rate.
Y. pestis, a Gram-negative coccobacillus belonging to the Enterobacteriaceae family.
Patients living in poverty whose housing is not rat proof are at increased risk.

Plague-infected flea bite leads to inoculation, followed by bacterial migration through cutaneous lymphatics to regional lymph nodes where they are phagocytosed but resist destruction (because of several virulence factors produced by the organism). They rapidly multiply, causing destruction and necrosis of lymph node architecture with subsequent bacteremia, septicemia, and endotoxemia that can quickly lead to shock, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and coma.
A small minority of patients infected by fleas develop Y. pestis septicemia without a discernible bubo, termed primary septicemic plague. Septicemia can also arise secondary to bubonic plague.
Primary pneumonic plague results from inhalation of droplets containing Y. pestis.

There is insufficient evidence to evaluate the effectiveness of any plague vaccine, or the relative effectiveness between vaccines and their tolerability. No evidence appears to exist on the long-term effects of any plague vaccine. C

When engaging in outdoor activities where plaque is endemic, use of long pants and insect repellant is advised as well as avoiding contact with ill or dead animals. Additionally, feeding of squirrels, chipmunks and other rodents should be avoided. C

Suspect plague when clinical symptoms, including fever and lymphadenopathy, are present in a person who resides in or has recently traveled to a plague-endemic area or when bipolar-staining coccobacilli are present on a smear from affected tissues (eg, a bubo, blood, tracheal, or lung aspirate).

Differential.Differential_Features: Moderately tender nodes compared with severe tenderness in plague
Course may be subacute or chronic compared with acute nature of plague
Selectively involves the inguinal lymph nodes
Typically more chronic in nature, associated with weight loss
Typically not as severely progressive as pneumonic plague
May be difficult to distinguish from primary septicemic plague
Typically nonproductive cough with temporary improvement initially

list.listitem: Patients typically develop symptoms of bubonic plague 2 to 8 days after being bitten by an infected flea. Symptoms include the sudden onset of fever, chills, weakness, and an acutely swollen and tender lymph node (bubo). The bubo is most frequently in the groin, axilla, or cervical region and is often so painful that it prevents patients from moving the affected area of the body. Buboes are 1 to 10 cm in diameter and the overlying skin is erythematous.
Septicemic plague may lead to disseminated intravascular coagulation, necrosis of small vessels, and purpuric skin lesions.
Gangrene of acral regions such as the digits and nose may also occur (and is thought to be responsible for the name "black death").
Patients with pneumonic plague have symptoms of severe bronchopneumonia, chest pain, dyspnea, cough, and hemoptysis.

Aspirate a bubo using a 20-gauge needle and a 10-mL syringe containing 1 to 2 mL of sterile saline for infusing the node. Obtain culture of bubo aspirate, blood, or sputum specimen (highly sensitive if patient is untreated and highly specific; results take 2-3 days).

Also order Gram stain or Wayson stain of bubo aspirate or sputum specimen to demonstrate bipolar staining. This test is only moderately sensitive and specific but provides results within minutes. Other testing (immunofluorescent antibody, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay [ELISA], or polymerase chain reaction [PCR]) depends on local availability.
Immunofluorescent antibody applied to bubo aspirate or sputum specimen is also an option if available. It is moderately sensitive, highly specific and also provides a result within minutes.
ELISA for F1 antigen in bubo aspirate is highly sensitive, highly specific, and provides results within hours.
Finally, PCR for F1 gene in bubo aspirate is moderately sensitive, highly specific, and also provides an answer within hours.
Plague should be suspected in a patient with fever and lymphadenopathy who resides in or has recently traveled to a plague-endemic area.
Aspirate the bubo and obtain culture, Gram stain, and other studies based on local availability.

When plague is suspected or diagnosed, contact hospital infection control and the health department. This will allow rapid arranging of definitive tests that may only be available through a state reference laboratory or the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and will allow early interventions to be instituted.

The preferred agent for treatment is intramuscular (IM) streptomycin 30 mg per kg per day (up to 1 g) given twice daily for 10 days or until 2 days after the patient's temperature has returned to normal. B

Asymptomatic persons having household, hospital, or other close contact with persons with untreated pneumatic plague should receive postexposure antibiotic prophylaxis for 7 days and be watched for fever and cough. C

The preferred agent for treatment is IM streptomycin 30 mg per kg per day (up to 1 g twice daily). The duration of treatment is 10 days or until 2 days after the patient's temperature has returned to normal.

Alternate agents include gentamicin 5 mg per kg IM or intravenously (IV) once daily, or a 2 mg per kg loading dose followed by 1.7 mg per kg every 8 hours; doxycycline 100 mg IV twice daily (or 200 mg once daily); chloramphenicol 25 mg per kg IV every 6 hours; or ciprofloxacin 400 mg IV or 500 mg oral twice daily.

Asymptomatic persons having household, hospital, or other close contact with persons with untreated pneumatic plague should receive postexposure antibiotic prophylaxis for 7 days and be watched for fever and cough. Close contact is defined as contact with the patient at less than 2 meters. Tetracycline, doxycycline, sulfonamides, and chloramphenicol have each been used or recommended as postexposure prophylaxis in this setting.

Patients with suspected pneumonic plague should be managed under respiratory droplet precautions until atleast 4 days of antibiotic treatment have been administered. For the otherclinical types of the disease, patients should be isolated for the first 48hours after the initiation of treatment.
Supportive care is an important part of the management, which may include immediate fluid resuscitation, vasopressors, hemodynamic monitoring, and respiratory care including ventilator support.
Rapid evolution of disease often occurs 2 to 4 days after symptom onset and without early treatment can lead to septic shock with high mortality.
Give gentamicin 5 mg per kg IM or IV once daily, or a 2 mg per kg loading dose followed by 1.7 mg per kg every 8 hours.
Preferred agents are streptomycin 15 mg per kg IM twice daily (maximum daily dose = 2 g) and gentamicin 2.5 mg per kg IM or IV every 8 hours.

Alternative agents include (1) doxycycline (for children older than 8 years): for those who weigh less than 45 kg = 2.2 mg per kg IV twice daily (maximum daily dose = 200 mg), and for those who weigh more than 45 kg = same dosage as adults; (2) ciprofloxacin 15 mg per kg IV twice daily (maximum daily dose = 1 g); and (3) chloramphenicol (for children older than 2 years): 25 mg per kg IV every 6 hours (maximum daily dose = 4 g).
